title: Fixed-Base Percentage
description: The fixed-base percentage is the historical ratio of research expenses to gross receipts that sets the Regular Research Credit's base amount.
summary: The fixed-base percentage (FBP) is the historical ratio of qualified research expenses to gross receipts that sets the base amount for the Regular Research Credit under IRC Section 41. U.S. taxpayers multiply it by prior four-year average gross receipts; it is capped at 16%, start-ups begin at 3%, and the base can never fall below 50% of current QREs.

body.text: The fixed-base percentage (FBP) is the historical ratio of qualified research expenses to gross receipts that sets the base amount for the Regular Research Credit under IRC Section 41. U.S. taxpayers multiply it by prior four-year average gross receipts; it is capped at 16%, start-ups begin at 3%, and the base can never fall below 50% of current QREs.

The Fixed-Base Percentage (FBP) is the foundational historical ratio governing the calculation of the Regular Research Credit (RRC) under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41). Within the RRC framework codified at 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1) and § 41(c), the FBP measures a taxpayer's historical research intensity—defined as aggregate Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) divided by aggregate Gross Receipts across a statutorily prescribed base period—and scales that ratio against the taxpayer's Average Annual Gross Receipts (AAGR) from the four immediately preceding taxable years to establish the Base Amount. Because 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1) awards a 20% gross tax credit strictly on current-year QREs that exceed this Base Amount (or 15.8% when a taxpayer elects the reduced credit under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c)), the FBP directly determines the revenue-indexed performance hurdle a business must clear to generate credit-eligible incremental research spending.

To balance historical benchmarking with ongoing incentives for domestic research investment, Congress bounded the FBP and Base Amount calculation with three core statutory rules: the FBP must be rounded to the nearest 1/100th of 1% (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(D)), the FBP cannot exceed a statutory ceiling of 16% (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(C)), and the resulting Base Amount can never be less than 50% of current-year QREs under the Minimum Base Amount Rule (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2)). For established ("non-startup") taxpayers, the FBP remains anchored to taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989 (the 1984–1988 base period) under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(A). Conversely, taxpayers meeting the statutory definition of a "start-up company" under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)(i) are assigned a fixed 3.00% FBP for their first five taxable years beginning after December 31, 1993, in which they incur QREs, followed by a phased transition across Years 6 through 10 to a permanent five-year historical ratio in Year 11 and thereafter under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)(ii). Whenever rapid R&D expansion or zero prior gross receipts cause a taxpayer's preliminary base calculation (FBP × AAGR) to fall below 50% of current-year QREs, the 50% statutory floor controls, yielding a maximum gross effective credit rate of 10.00% of total current-year QREs (20% × 50%) prior to any IRC § 280C(c) adjustment. Notably, while Public Law 119-21 (enacted July 4, 2025) amended 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) and § 280C(c) to coordinate qualified research with domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, Congress left the Fixed-Base Percentage and Base Amount architecture in 26 U.S.C. § 41(c) intact.
Statutory Foundation and Mechanics of the Fixed-Base Percentage in the Regular Research Credit
Establishing the Historical Base Period (1984–1988) and Look-Back Requirements

The Regular Research Credit (RRC) under 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1) is structured as an incremental tax incentive that rewards a taxpayer solely to the extent its current-year QREs exceed a historically anchored Base Amount. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(1), the term "base amount" is defined statutorily as the product of two distinct components: (A) the taxpayer's Fixed-Base Percentage (FBP), and (B) the taxpayer's Average Annual Gross Receipts (AAGR) for the four taxable years immediately preceding the taxable year for which the credit is being determined (statutorily designated as the "credit year"). By coupling a fixed historical research-intensity ratio with a rolling four-year revenue multiplier for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1989 (enacted under Pub. L. 101-239), Congress replaced the prior rolling base period—under which increasing current R&D outlays automatically penalized future base computations—while still requiring research spending to scale alongside recent business revenue.

For established taxpayers—specifically, taxpayers that do not fall within the statutory definition of a "start-up company" under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)(i)—the FBP is governed by the general rule of 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(A). That subparagraph mandates that the FBP is the percentage which the taxpayer's aggregate QREs for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989 (the 1984–1988 fixed-base period) is of the taxpayer's aggregate gross receipts for those exact same taxable years:

Pursuant to 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(D), the percentage determined under subparagraph (A) (as well as under subparagraph (B)(ii) for start-up companies) must be rounded to the nearest 1/100th of 1 percent—meaning two decimal places when expressed as a percentage, such as 2.50%, or four decimal places when expressed as a decimal ratio on tax workpapers, such as 0.0250. Because the statutory formula computes a ratio of five-year aggregates (∑ QREs ÷ ∑ Gross Receipts) rather than an unweighted average of five annual percentages, higher-revenue years within the 1984–1988 base period carry proportionally greater mathematical weight in fixing the permanent FBP.
Gross Receipts Definition and Short Taxable Year Rules (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(6) & 26 CFR § 1.41-3)

Because gross receipts form both the denominator of the FBP ratio and the four-year preceding AAGR multiplier, accurate FBP compliance depends on strict adherence to the statutory and regulatory definition of gross receipts. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(6) and Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(1) (promulgated in T.D. 8930, 66 FR 289, effective for taxable years beginning on or after January 3, 2001), "gross receipts" means the total amount, as determined under the taxpayer's method of accounting, derived by the taxpayer from all its activities and from all sources, such as revenues derived from the sale of inventory before reduction for cost of goods sold.

However, 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(6) and 26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(2)(i)–(vi) explicitly exclude six categories of items from gross receipts when computing both the FBP and the four-year preceding AAGR. Specifically, gross receipts exclude: (i) returns or allowances under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(6) and 26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(2)(i); (ii) receipts from the sale or exchange of capital assets as defined in IRC § 1221 under 26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(2)(ii); (iii) repayments of loans or similar instruments, such as the repayment of loan principal held by a commercial lender, under 26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(2)(iii); (iv) receipts from a sale or exchange not in the ordinary course of business, such as the sale of an entire trade or business or the sale of property used in a trade or business as defined under IRC § 1221(2), under 26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(2)(iv); (v) amounts received with respect to state and local sales taxes or similar taxes if, under applicable state or local law, the tax is legally imposed on the purchaser of the good or service and the taxpayer merely collects and remits the tax to the taxing authority, under 26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(2)(v); and (vi) amounts received by a taxpayer in a taxable year that precedes the first taxable year in which the taxpayer derives more than $25,000 in gross receipts other than investment income—where investment income is defined as interest or distributions with respect to stock other than the stock of a 20-percent owned corporation as defined in IRC § 243(c)(2)—under 26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(2)(vi).

For foreign corporations claiming the U.S. research credit, 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(6) and 26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(3) restrict gross receipts solely to gross receipts that are effectively connected with the conduct of a trade or business within the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or other possessions of the United States, cross-referencing IRC § 864(c) and the regulations thereunder. Equally critical are the asymmetrical short taxable year rules codified under 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(4) and 26 CFR § 1.41-3(b)(1)–(3). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-3(b)(3) and Chapter 3 of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide, no adjustment is made on account of a short taxable year when computing a taxpayer's Fixed-Base Percentage, because any shortened accounting period within the base period affects both the QRE numerator and the gross-receipts denominator over the same duration. Conversely, if the credit year itself is a short taxable year, 26 CFR § 1.41-3(b)(1) requires modifying the Preliminary Base Amount determined under section 41(c)(1)—but explicitly not the 50% Minimum Base Amount floor under section 41(c)(2)—by multiplying that amount by the number of months in the short taxable year and dividing the result by 12. Similarly, if one or more of the four taxable years immediately preceding the credit year is a short taxable year, 26 CFR § 1.41-3(b)(2) requires annualizing the gross receipts for each such short year by multiplying the gross receipts actually derived in that year by 12 and dividing by the number of months in that year.
Administrative Burden of the Fixed 1984–1988 Base Period

Anchoring the standard non-startup FBP permanently to the 1984–1988 window imposes a substantial archival and forensic accounting burden on legacy corporate enterprises more than four decades later. Established taxpayers claiming the 20% RRC under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(A) must retain, access, and validate forty-year-old general ledgers, chart-of-accounts structures, tax returns, and organizational histories across decades of accounting system migrations and corporate restructurings. Consequently, Chapters 3, 6, and 7 of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide instruct examiners to scrutinize base-period workpapers and evaluate whether the claimed 1984–1988 FBP is substantially lower than current research ratios without a documented historical explanation.
Determining the Base Amount, Statutory Constraints, and Form 6765 Mechanics

Once the historical FBP is established and rounded to the nearest 0.01% under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(D), it is multiplied by the taxpayer's four-year preceding AAGR to produce the Preliminary Base Amount under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(1).

Two overarching statutory constraints govern the application of the FBP and the resulting Operative Base Amount. First, under the Maximum Fixed-Base Percentage Cap codified at 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(C), "[i]n no event shall the fixed-base percentage exceed 16 percent" (0.16). Regardless of how high a taxpayer's historical QRE-to-gross-receipts ratio was during the base period, this statutory ceiling prevents historically research-intensive firms from being assigned a prohibitive FBP that would permanently disqualify them from claiming the RRC. Second, under the Minimum Base Amount Floor codified at 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2), "[i]n no event shall the base amount be less than 50 percent of the qualified research expenses for the credit year". Thus, the Operative Base Amount is always the greater of the Preliminary Base Amount (FBP × AAGR) or the Minimum Base Amount (50% × Current-Year QREs).

The interaction between the 16% FBP cap and the 50% Minimum Base Amount floor defines the operational boundaries of the RRC. While the 16% cap limits the maximum historical hurdle relative to prior four-year revenue, the 50% floor ensures that at least half of current-year QREs are absorbed into the non-creditable base—capping eligible incremental QREs at 50% of total current-year QREs and capping the maximum gross RRC at 10.00% of total current-year QREs (20% statutory rate × 50% maximum incremental QREs, or 7.90% of total QREs if the 15.8% reduced credit under IRC § 280C(c) is elected). Conversely, whenever the Preliminary Base Amount exceeds 50% of current-year QREs—which occurs whenever the FBP exceeds the critical inflection threshold (0.50 × Current-Year QREs) ÷ Prior 4-Year AAGR—the historical FBP becomes the binding marginal constraint, reducing incremental QREs dollar-for-dollar against AAGR until current-year QREs no longer exceed FBP × AAGR.
Implementation on IRS Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024 / Instructions Rev. December 2025)

On the redesigned IRS Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities, bearing form revision date Rev. December 2024 on the PDF form and referenced as the January 2025 revision in the Instructions for Form 6765, Rev. December 2025), the FBP and Base Amount rules in Section A (Regular Credit) are executed across Lines 5 through 13, replacing the pre-2024 line numbering where the FBP appeared on Line 10 and AAGR appeared on Line 11. In addition, header Item A at the top of Form 6765 records the taxpayer's timely original-return election of the reduced credit under IRC § 280C (replacing pre-2024 Box 17 or Box 34), while header Item B records whether the taxpayer is a member of a controlled group or business under common control. As tax practitioner commentary notes, although IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-28 (issued August 28, 2025, under Public Law 119-21) created a temporary exception allowing eligible small businesses meeting the IRC § 448(c) gross receipts test ($31 million or less) making retroactive Section 174A elections to file late or revoked Section 280C elections for 2022–2024 until the earlier of July 6, 2026, or the refund statute of limitations, that transition window has closed as of November 2026, leaving the irrevocable original-return requirement in force.

Rather than printing a single line labeled "Operative Base Amount," Section A of Form 6765 enforces the 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2) 50% Minimum Base Amount floor by comparing Preliminary Excess QREs over the Preliminary Base Amount (Line 9) against 50% of current-year QREs (Line 10) and requiring the taxpayer to enter the smaller of those two figures on Line 11. Because min(QREs − Preliminary Base, 0.50 × QREs) is algebraically equivalent to max(0, QREs − max(Preliminary Base, 0.50 × QREs)) when positive, Line 11 enforces the 50% statutory floor directly. Note that for a member of a controlled group filing a separate return, the December 2025 Instructions for Form 6765 direct the filer to enter only the individual member's QREs on Line 5 and the group-wide FBP on Line 6, while computing the group credit and allocated member share on the mandatory Item B attachment (Form6765ItemBGroupCredit.pdf) and entering the member's allocated share on Line 13.

body.text: Hypothetical Worked Examples: Fixed-Base Percentage and Base Amount Mechanics

To illustrate how the Fixed-Base Percentage interacts with the four-year preceding AAGR, the 16.00% statutory cap (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(C)), and the 50% Minimum Base Amount floor (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2)), the worked examples and comparative table below trace the statutory mechanics of 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1) and § 41(c)(1)–(3) across Section A of IRS Form 6765.
Hypothetical Worked Example 1: Established Taxpayer Operating at the 50% Minimum Base Amount Threshold

In this hypothetical scenario, the taxpayer has Current-Year QREs (2023) of $1,000,000 (reported on Form 6765, Section F, Line 48 and carried to Section A, Line 5), a Historical Fixed-Base Percentage (1984–1988 QRE-to-Gross-Receipts Ratio) of 2.50% (0.0250, rounded to the nearest 1/100th of 1% under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(D) and confirmed to be below the 16.00% maximum cap under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(C), entered on Form 6765, Line 6), and Average Annual Gross Receipts (AAGR) for the Preceding 4 Tax Years (2019–2022) of $20,000,000 (entered on Form 6765, Line 7).
Recomputing the credit step-by-step under 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1) and § 41(c)(1)–(3) and mapping each step to Section A of Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024) yields the following results:

items: Compute the Preliminary Base Amount (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(1); Form 6765, Line 8): Multiply the 4-year preceding AAGR ($20,000,000, Line 7) by the FBP (2.50% or 0.0250, Line 6), which equals $500,000 ($20,000,000 × 0.0250 = $500,000).

Compute Preliminary Excess QREs (Form 6765, Line 9): Subtract the Preliminary Base Amount ($500,000, Line 8) from Current-Year QREs ($1,000,000, Line 5), which equals $500,000 ($1,000,000 − $500,000 = $500,000).

Compute the 50% Minimum Base Amount / Maximum Creditable QRE Ceiling (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2); Form 6765, Line 10): Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2), the Base Amount cannot be less than 50% of Current-Year QREs (0.50 × $1,000,000 = $500,000). Correspondingly, Line 10 of Form 6765 multiplies Line 5 QREs ($1,000,000) by 50% (0.50), entering $500,000.

Determine Operative Base Amount and Eligible Incremental QREs (Form 6765, Line 11): Comparing the Preliminary Base Amount ($500,000) against the Minimum Base Amount ($500,000), both thresholds sit at $500,000. On Form 6765, Line 11 enters the smaller of Line 9 ($500,000) or Line 10 ($500,000), resulting in $500,000 of credit-eligible incremental QREs.

Compute the Regular Research Credit (26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1); Form 6765, Lines 12–13): Assuming no energy consortium or basic research payments on Lines 1–4 (so Line 12 = $500,000) and no IRC § 280C(c) reduced credit election, multiply the incremental QREs ($500,000) by the 20% (0.20) statutory credit rate on Line 13 to produce a gross Regular Research Credit of $100,000 ($500,000 × 0.20 = $100,000), representing an effective gross credit rate of 10.00% on total current-year QREs ($100,000 ÷ $1,000,000)—or $79,000 ($500,000 × 0.158, a 7.90% effective rate) if electing the reduced credit under IRC § 280C(c).

body.text: Hypothetical Worked Example 2: Sensitivity of the Base Amount to FBP Variations Above and Below the 50% Floor

To see why the FBP is strategically decisive—and how the 50% Minimum Base Amount floor (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2)) and the 16.00% statutory cap (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(C)) create distinct marginal regimes—consider three additional hypothetical scenarios evaluated step-by-step under the statutory rules.

In Hypothetical Scenario A (Low FBP Overridden by the 50% Floor), assume the same $1,000,000 in current QREs and $20,000,000 in 4-year preceding AAGR, but a lower historical FBP of 1.50% (0.0150). The Preliminary Base Amount on Line 8 falls to $300,000 ($20,000,000 × 0.0150), raising Line 9 Preliminary Excess QREs to $700,000 ($1,000,000 − $300,000). However, because 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2) floors the Base Amount at 50% of current QREs ($500,000 on Line 10), Line 11 caps eligible incremental QREs at $500,000, and the 20% gross RRC remains unchanged at $100,000. As explicitly noted in Chapter 6 of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide under audit risk analysis, when a taxpayer's Base Amount is already governed by the 50% limitation rule, a modest upward examination adjustment to the FBP—for instance, increasing the FBP from 1.50% to 2.25%, which raises the Preliminary Base Amount from $300,000 to $450,000—has no effect on the final tax credit because the $500,000 floor continues to bind until the FBP exceeds 2.50% ((0.50 × $1,000,000) ÷ $20,000,000 = 2.50%).

Here, the inflection threshold where the 50% floor yields control to the FBP is 7.50% ((0.50 × $1,500,000) ÷ $10,000,000 = 7.50%). Because the 10.00% FBP exceeds 7.50%, the Preliminary Base Amount on Line 8 is $1,000,000 ($10,000,000 × 0.1000), which exceeds the 50% Minimum Base Amount floor of $750,000 (0.50 × $1,500,000 on Line 10). Consequently, the FBP-driven Preliminary Base Amount ($1,000,000) is the operative constraint, reducing eligible incremental QREs on Line 9 and Line 11 to $500,000 ($1,500,000 − $1,000,000) and yielding a 20% gross RRC of $100,000—an effective rate of 6.67% on total current-year QREs.

In Hypothetical Scenario C (High FBP Capped at 16.00% Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(C)), suppose a legacy technology firm had $5,000,000 in aggregate 1984–1988 QREs and $25,000,000 in aggregate 1984–1988 gross receipts, yielding an unadjusted historical ratio of 20.00% ($5,000,000 ÷ $25,000,000), alongside $10,000,000 in 4-year preceding AAGR and $2,000,000 in current-year QREs. Without a statutory cap, its Preliminary Base Amount would be $2,000,000 ($10,000,000 × 0.2000), eliminating its incremental QREs ($2,000,000 − $2,000,000 = $0). Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(C) and Form 6765 Line 6, however, its FBP is capped at 16.00% (0.16), fixing its Preliminary Base Amount at $1,600,000 ($10,000,000 × 0.1600). Because $1,600,000 exceeds the 50% floor ($1,000,000 on Line 10), the taxpayer retains $400,000 in incremental QREs ($2,000,000 − $1,600,000) and earns an $80,000 gross RRC ($400,000 × 0.20, a 4.00% effective rate on total QREs).
Fixed-Base Percentage Rules for Start-Up Companies (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B))
Statutory Definition of a Start-Up Company

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)(i)(I)–(II) and the IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025, Line 6), a taxpayer's FBP must be determined under the start-up company rules if either of the following two disjunctive conditions is met:

items: Post-1983 First Dual-Activity Year (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)(i)(I)): The first taxable year in which the taxpayer had both gross receipts and qualified research expenses begins after December 31, 1983; OR

Fewer Than Three Dual-Activity Years in 1984–1988 (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)(i)(II)): There are fewer than 3 taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989, in which the taxpayer had both gross receipts and qualified research expenses.

body.text: As documented in the historical amendment notes to 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)(i), Congress originally enacted only Prong (II) in 1993, but amended § 41(c)(3)(B)(i) in the Small Business Job Protection Act of 1996 (Pub. L. 104-188, § 1204(b)) to add Prong (I). Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-6(b)(2)(ii) Example illustrates the decisive legal consequence of Prong (I): if a calendar-year company was formed in 1984 (or earlier without dual activity) and incurred both QREs and gross receipts in all five years from 1984 through 1988, it is still statutorily classified as a start-up company on a standalone basis under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)(i)(I) because the first taxable year in which it had both QREs and gross receipts began after December 31, 1983. Thus, a taxpayer is an established ("non-startup") company subject to the 1984–1988 FBP under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(A) if and only if (a) it had both gross receipts and QREs in at least one taxable year beginning before January 1, 1984, and (b) it also had both gross receipts and QREs in at least three taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989. Furthermore, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)(iii), the Secretary of the Treasury is authorized to prescribe regulations disregarding de minimis amounts of gross receipts and QREs under clauses (i) and (ii), complementing the $25,000 non-investment gross-receipts exclusion in 26 CFR § 1.41-3(c)(2)(vi).
The Initial 3.00% Fixed-Base Percentage (Years 1–5) and the Zero Gross Receipts Rule

For any taxpayer qualifying as a start-up company under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)(i), clause (ii)(I) assigns a statutory Fixed-Base Percentage of 3 percent (3.00%) for each of the taxpayer's first 5 taxable years beginning after December 31, 1993, for which the taxpayer has qualified research expenses. Under the plain statutory language of clause (ii)(I) and 26 CFR § 1.41-6(b)(2)(iii)–(iv), taxable years beginning on or before December 31, 1993, do not count toward this five-year period, and only post-1993 taxable years in which the taxpayer actually incurs QREs advance the five-year clock—meaning intervening years with zero QREs are skipped rather than exhausting the 3.00% window.

The 3.00% statutory FBP provides two major benefits to early-stage and pre-revenue enterprises. First, it eliminates any requirement to locate or reconstruct 1980s financial records. Second, it interacts favorably with the new-taxpayer AAGR conventions in Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-3(a) and the 50% Minimum Base Amount floor in 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-3(a), if a new taxpayer has not been in existence for any previous taxable year, its AAGR for the four preceding taxable years is zero ($0); if it has been in existence for one, two, or three preceding taxable years, its AAGR is the average annual gross receipts over the exact number of preceding taxable years for which it has been in existence, without excluding existence years in which gross receipts were $0. Whenever a start-up company in Years 1–5 has $0 AAGR across its preceding existence years, its Preliminary Base Amount (3.00% × $0) equals $0, causing the 50% Minimum Base Amount rule of 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(2) to govern and generate a gross Regular Research Credit equal to 10.00% of total current-year QREs:

As explained in AICPA The Tax Adviser (April 2012) and codified in 26 U.S.C. § 39(a)(1), even if a pre-revenue start-up has no current income tax liability against which to offset this credit, unused general business credits carry back 1 year and carry forward for 20 years (with a deduction allowed in the 21st year for unused amounts under IRC § 196, as noted in The Tax Adviser December 2018). In addition, a qualified small business under 26 U.S.C. § 41(h) may elect on Section D of Form 6765 to apply up to $500,000 annually of its research credit against employer payroll taxes for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022.
The Moving-Average Transition Formula (Years 6–10) and Permanent Base Selection (Year 11+)

Beginning in the 6th taxable year (beginning after December 31, 1993) for which a start-up company has QREs, 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)(ii)(II)–(VII) replaces the flat 3.00% rate with a multi-stage transition schedule that progressively phases in the taxpayer's actual historical ratio of QREs to gross receipts.

In this statutory phase-in equation for qualifying QRE years 6 through 10, designates the prescribed look-back subset of prior post-1993 QRE taxable years and represents the corresponding statutory multiplier (1/6 for Year 6, 1/3 for Year 7, 1/2 for Year 8, 2/3 for Year 9, and 5/6 for Year 10).

The statutory transition incorporates two deliberate structural features designed to protect growing companies from early-stage volatility while transitioning them toward a permanent historical benchmark. First, none of the transition formulas in Years 6 through 11+ ever include QREs or gross receipts from the taxpayer's 1st, 2nd, or 3rd post-1993 QRE years, and Year 4 is used solely in Year 6 before being permanently dropped in Year 7 and all subsequent years under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)(ii)(II)–(VII). Excluding these earliest pre-commercialization years prevents extreme initial R&D-to-revenue ratios from permanently inflating the taxpayer's long-term FBP. Second, beginning in the 11th post-1993 taxable year with QREs and for all taxable years thereafter under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)(ii)(VII), the taxpayer computes its FBP using 100% of the aggregate QREs divided by aggregate gross receipts for any 5 taxable years selected by the taxpayer from among the 5th through the 10th such taxable years. This selection rule enables a mature start-up to evaluate all six five-year combinations among Years 5 through 10 and exclude whichever single year produces the least favorable weighted ratio, locking in the lowest compliant FBP. Across every transition and post-transition year, the resulting percentage must be rounded to the nearest 0.01% under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(D) and capped at 16.00% under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(C), although—as noted in the compliance recommendations below—current Form 6765 Line 6 instructions do not provide an explicit worked example for cases where aggregate gross receipts remain $0 across an entire Year 6–10 look-back window.

body.text: Controlled Group Aggregation, Acquisitions, and Dispositions (26 U.S.C. § 41(f))
Mandatory Controlled Group Aggregation and Credit Allocation (26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-6)

To prevent affiliated corporate structures from artificially isolating QREs in one entity and gross receipts in another to manipulate the Fixed-Base Percentage or AAGR, 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(1) mandates single-taxpayer aggregation across all commonly controlled entities. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(1)(A)(i), all members of the same controlled group of corporations must be treated as a single taxpayer in determining the amount of the research credit. Pursuant to 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(5), the term "controlled group of corporations" carries the meaning set forth in IRC § 1563(a), except that "more than 50 percent" common ownership is substituted for "at least 80 percent" each place it appears in IRC § 1563(a)(1) (§ 41(f)(5)(A)), and the determination is made without regard to IRC § 1563(a)(4) and (e)(3)(C) (§ 41(f)(5)(B)). Parallel rules under 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(1)(B)(i) and 26 CFR § 1.41-6(a)(3)(ii) and (v) (cross-referencing 26 CFR § 1.52-1(b)–(g)) require that all trades or businesses—whether or not incorporated, including sole proprietorships, partnerships, trusts, estates, and corporations—under common control at the end of the member's taxable year be treated as a single taxpayer, deeming any corporate member to be carrying on a trade or business if any other member of that group carries on a trade or business.
Group-Wide Fixed-Base Percentage and Start-Up Status (26 CFR § 1.41-6(b))

Because all controlled group members are treated as a single taxpayer under 26 CFR § 1.41-6(b)(1), the Fixed-Base Percentage, four-year preceding AAGR, Preliminary Base Amount, and 50% Minimum Base Amount floor must all be computed on an aggregate group-wide basis. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-6(i)(1)–(5), intra-group transfers are generally disregarded so that intercompany research services, leases, and supply transfers do not duplicate gross receipts or QREs; for instance, when one group member performs in-house research on behalf of another member, the performing member includes its in-house research expenses in QREs without treating intercompany reimbursement as funding, while the paying member excludes the payment from contract research expenses. Moreover, all members of the controlled group must use the exact same computation method—either the Regular Research Credit under § 41(a)(1) or the Alternative Simplified Credit—for the credit year, bound by the designated member's election or revocation (26 CFR § 1.41-6(b)(1); § 1.41-9(b)(4)), and group members filing separate returns must enter the group-wide FBP on Line 6 of Form 6765.

Crucially, Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-6(b)(2)(i) establishes special aggregation rules for determining whether a controlled group qualifies as a start-up company under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(3)(B)(i). A controlled group is treated as a start-up company only if (A) there was no taxable year beginning before January 1, 1984, in which a member of the group had gross receipts and either the same member or another member also had QREs, or (B) there were fewer than three taxable years beginning after December 31, 1983, and before January 1, 1989, in which a member of the group had gross receipts and either the same member or another member had QREs. As illustrated in 26 CFR § 1.41-6(b)(2)(ii) Example, if calendar-year Member A had QREs (but no gross receipts) in 1983, Member B had gross receipts (but no QREs) in 1983, Member C had neither in 1983, and A, B, and C each had both QREs and gross receipts in 1984 through 1988, each entity would qualify as a start-up company on a standalone basis because none individually had dual activity before 1984; however, the controlled group as a whole is not a start-up company because the group collectively had both QREs (via A) and gross receipts (via B) in 1983 and in at least three years during 1984–1988. Conversely, if a controlled group (or consolidated group under § 1.41-6(d)(2)) does qualify as a start-up company, 26 CFR § 1.41-6(b)(2)(iii) and (iv) Example establish that the group's first taxable year after December 31, 1993, with QREs—starting the five-year clock for the 3.00% FBP—is the first post-1993 taxable year in which at least one member of the group incurs QREs.
Group Credit Allocation (26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(1) & 26 CFR § 1.41-6(c))

Subsequently, in Pub. L. 112-240, § 301(c) (applicable to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2011), Congress amended 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(1)(A)(ii) and (B)(ii) to mandate that the credit allowable to each member be determined on a proportionate basis to its share of the aggregate QREs, basic research payments, and amounts paid or incurred to energy research consortiums taken into account by the controlled group. Following temporary regulations in T.D. 9717 (80 FR 23237), Treasury promulgated current final 26 CFR § 1.41-6(c) in T.D. 9832 (83 FR 13183, March 28, 2018; effective and applicable to taxable years beginning on or after April 2, 2018, under § 1.41-6(j)(4)). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-6(c), (d)(1), (d)(3), and (e) Examples 1 and 2, the group credit is allocated directly in proportion to each member's share of aggregate current-year QREs (collectively encompassing QREs, basic research payments, and energy consortium payments), with members of a consolidated return group treated initially as a single combined member of the controlled group under § 1.41-6(d)(1) and their combined share then sub-allocated proportionately among the consolidated members under § 1.41-6(d)(3). Under the Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025, Item B), any filer checking "Yes" to Item B must attach a schedule—named Form6765ItemBGroupCredit.pdf for e-filed returns—reporting 12 required columns for each member (Entity EIN, Entity Name, Common Parent/Designated Member, Consolidated Member, PBA Code, Wages QREs, Supplies QREs, Rent/Lease Computers QREs, Contract Research QREs, Total QREs of Controlled Member, Percentage of credit, and Portion of credit reflecting any Item A Section 280C reduction), concluding with total controlled-group QREs and credit plus disclosures of current- vs. prior-year member counts and consolidated vs. separate return filing status.
Impact of Mergers, Acquisitions, and Dispositions on the Fixed-Base Percentage (26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(3))
Specifically, 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(3) establishes three interlocking adjustment rules for transactions occurring after December 31, 1983:

items: Acquisitions (26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(3)(A)): If a taxpayer acquires the major portion of a trade or business of another person (the "predecessor") or the major portion of a separate unit of a trade or business of a predecessor, then in applying IRC § 41 for taxable years ending after the acquisition, both the QREs and the gross receipts of the acquiring taxpayer for periods before the acquisition (encompassing both the 1984–1988 FBP base period—or start-up base years—and the four preceding AAGR years) must be increased by the predecessor's QREs and gross receipts attributable to the acquired portion.

Dispositions (26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(3)(B)): Reciprocally, if after December 31, 1983, a taxpayer disposes of the major portion of any trade or business (or separate unit thereof) in a transaction to which § 41(f)(3)(A) applies, and the disposing taxpayer furnishes the acquiring person such information as is necessary for the application of § 41(f)(3)(A) (§ 41(f)(3)(B)(ii)), then the disposing taxpayer's QREs and gross receipts for periods before the disposition are decreased by the amounts attributable to the disposed portion.

Post-Disposition Research Reimbursements Affecting FBP (26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(3)(C)): If, during any of the 3 taxable years following the taxable year of a disposition under § 41(f)(3)(B), the disposing taxpayer (or a commonly controlled member) reimburses the acquiring person for research performed on behalf of the disposing taxpayer, the disposing taxpayer must increase its QREs for the taxable years taken into account in computing its Fixed-Base Percentage by the lesser of: (i) the amount of the § 41(f)(3)(B) QRE decrease allocable to those FBP base years, or (ii) the product of the number of taxable years taken into account in computing the FBP multiplied by the amount of the reimbursement.

body.text: Critical Distinction Between Asset/Business Acquisitions (§ 41(f)(3)) and Standalone Stock Acquisitions (§ 41(f)(1))

Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-7(b) cross-references paragraph (b) of 26 CFR § 1.52-2 for the definitions of "acquisition," "separate unit," and "major portion," specifying further that an "acquisition" includes an incorporation or a liquidation. Importantly, Chapter 3 of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (Section 3.e(3), Acquisitions/dispositions, updated July 2, 2026) underscores a vital technical distinction for M&A due diligence: the acquisition of the stock of another company, or disposition of stock, standing alone, does not trigger application of 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(3). Instead, when a corporation acquires or disposes of more than 50% of the stock of a subsidiary without liquidating or merging its underlying assets, the target enters or exits the taxpayer's controlled group, and its historical base-period QREs and gross receipts are aggregated into (or removed from) the group's single-taxpayer FBP computation via the controlled group aggregation rules of 26 U.S.C. § 41(f)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-6 rather than the separate-unit adjustment and seller information-furnishing rules of § 41(f)(3). Under either structural pathway, acquisitive corporations claiming the RRC must identify, verify, and retain historical QRE and gross receipt records for all acquired businesses and predecessors from the 1984–1988 base years through the current credit year.
Strategic Comparison with the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) and IRS Audit Substantiation
Evaluating the Fixed-Base Percentage Against the Alternative Simplified Credit (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4) and 26 CFR § 1.41-9)

Because substantiating a forty-year-old 1984–1988 Fixed-Base Percentage—or overcoming a high historical research ratio combined with rapid revenue expansion—frequently prevents legacy taxpayers from claiming the 20% Regular Research Credit, Congress enacted the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) in the Tax Relief and Health Care Act of 2006 (Pub. L. 109-432, effective for taxable years ending after December 31, 2006).
Statutory Redesignation Note (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4) vs. Former § 41(c)(5))

While Pub. L. 109-432 originally enacted the ASC as IRC § 41(c)(5), Congress subsequently repealed the expired Alternative Incremental Research Credit (AIRC, formerly § 41(c)(4), which applied only to taxable years beginning on or before December 31, 2008) and redesignated former paragraphs (c)(5), (c)(6), and (c)(7) in the United States Code as current 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4) (Election of alternative simplified credit), § 41(c)(5) (Consistent treatment of expenses required), and § 41(c)(6) (Gross receipts). Because the Treasury Department has not yet amended the internal cross-references in 26 CFR § 1.41-6(b)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-9, the regulatory text still refers to the ASC as section 41(c)(5) and the consistency rule as section 41(c)(6). Both citations appear in practitioner literature, as noted by Strike Tax Advisory, but the controlling statutory designation in the current United States Code is 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4).
ASC Mechanics, Election Rules, and Strategic Trade-Offs Against the FBP

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4)(A) and IRS Form 6765 Section B (Lines 14–26), a taxpayer electing the ASC bypasses both the Fixed-Base Percentage (1984–1988 base period or start-up transition) and the four-year preceding AAGR. Under the standard ASC calculation (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4)(A); Form 6765, Lines 20–24), the gross credit equals 14% (0.14) of so much of the taxpayer's current-year QREs (Line 20) as exceeds 50% of the average QREs for the 3 preceding taxable years—computed on Form 6765 by summing the prior 3 years' QREs on Line 21 and dividing by 6.0 on Line 22, since (Sum of Prior 3 Years' QREs ÷ 3) × 50% = Sum of Prior 3 Years' QREs ÷ 6.0. However, under the mandatory fallback rule of 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-9(c)(1) (Form 6765, Line 21 and Line 24), if the taxpayer had no QREs in any one of the 3 preceding taxable years, the taxpayer skips Lines 22 and 23 and computes a gross credit equal to 6% (0.06) of current-year QREs. If the taxpayer elects the reduced credit under IRC § 280C(c) on Item A, Form 6765 Line 26 multiplies Line 25 by 79% (0.79), producing an effective marginal rate of 11.06% (14% × 0.79) above the three-year base, or 4.74% (6% × 0.79) under the zero-prior-year rule.

Choosing between the FBP-based RRC and the ASC involves sharp quantitative and procedural trade-offs. Early-stage start-up companies in Years 1 through 5 generally realize a substantially higher credit under the RRC, where the 3.00% start-up FBP and 50% Minimum Base Amount floor yield a 10.00% gross effective rate on QREs, compared to 6.00% under the ASC when lacking QREs in any of the prior three years or 7.00% (14% × (1 − 0.50)) when QREs are flat across four years. Conversely, as Chapter 3 of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide highlights, established companies experiencing rapid growth in gross receipts alongside flat R&D outlays often find their RRC Base Amount (FBP × AAGR) exceeding current-year QREs—eliminating the RRC entirely—whereas the ASC ignores gross receipts and preserves a positive credit. Procedurally, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-9(b)(1)–(3), an ASC election applies to the election year and all succeeding taxable years unless revoked by claiming the RRC in Section A on a timely filed (including extensions) original return; while 26 CFR § 1.41-9(b)(2) permits an ASC election on an amended return for an open year only if neither the taxpayer nor any controlled-group member previously claimed a § 41(a)(1) credit under another method for that year, an existing ASC election can never be revoked on an amended return, nor is relief under 26 CFR § 301.9100-3 available. Note also that for short taxable years, 26 CFR § 1.41-9(c)(3)(i) requires daily proration/annualization (multiplying or dividing by 365) under the ASC, in contrast to monthly proration/annualization (multiplying or dividing by 12) for the RRC Base Amount under 26 CFR § 1.41-3(b)(1)–(2).

body.text: IRS Examination Focus: The Consistency Requirement (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(5)) and Base Period Substantiation

Chapter 3 of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (updated July 2, 2026) explicitly advises examiners that in many instances, verifying the base amount computation can have a more significant impact on audit results than determining allowable credit-year QREs, making mechanical review of the base computation mandatory in all examinations.
The Statutory Consistency Requirement (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(5)(A) & 26 CFR § 1.41-3(d))

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(5)(A) and Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-3(d)(1), in computing the research credit for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1989, the QREs and gross receipts taken into account in computing a taxpayer's Fixed-Base Percentage and Base Amount must be determined on a basis consistent with the definition and determination of QREs and gross receipts for the credit year, without regard to the law in effect for the taxable years taken into account in computing the FBP or Base Amount. Furthermore, this consistency mandate applies regardless of whether the statutory period of limitations for filing a claim for credit or refund has expired for any base-period taxable year, and Chapter 6 of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide confirms that consistency requires symmetrical treatment both between credit-year QREs and base-year QREs and between base-year gross receipts and the preceding four-year AAGR.

Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-3(d)(2) provides two concrete illustrations of how the consistency rule operates bilaterally. In 26 CFR § 1.41-3(d)(2) Example 1 (Downward Base Adjustment), calendar-year accrual Taxpayer X computes its research credit for 2001 after having reported $100x (1984), $120x (1985), $150x (1986), $180x (1987), and $170x (1988)—totaling $720x—as QREs on its 1984–1988 Forms 6765 based on the statutory definition of qualified research in effect for those years. Because Congress narrowed the statutory definition of qualified research for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1985, applying the credit-year definition retroactively to 1984 and 1985 reduces X's allowable QREs for those two years to $80x and $100x, respectively; under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(5) and 26 CFR § 1.41-3(d)(1), X must reduce its 1984–1988 aggregate base-period QREs from $720x to $680x ($80x + $100x + $150x + $180x + $170x = $680x) when computing its FBP. Conversely, in 26 CFR § 1.41-3(d)(2) Example 2 (Upward Base Adjustment), if Taxpayer X newly claims in the credit year that a particular category of expenditure qualifies as a QRE—reflecting a change in position because X had not previously treated similar expenditures as QREs—the consistency rule compels X to increase its 1984–1988 QREs in the numerator of its FBP to include any similar expenditures paid or incurred during the 1984–1988 fixed-base period, even though those base years are closed by the statute of limitations.
IRS Audit Procedures, Case Law Precedent, and Initial IDR Substantiation (I.R.C. § 6001)
Chapter 6 (The Consistency Requirement, updated July 2, 2026) of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide establishes four core diagnostic questions for auditing a taxpayer's FBP:

items: "Is the fixed-base percentage (the ratio of 84-88 QREs to gross receipts) in the base years substantially lower than current research ratios? If so, why?"
"Do past annual reports or 10Ks support the reported base years' QREs?"
"If the research credit was claimed in prior years, were the same base years' attributes used? If not, why not?"
"Was there a prior research credit examination? Did it cover one or more of the base years?"

body.text: Crucially, ATG Chapter 6 instructs examiners that taxpayers may not rely upon mathematical extrapolation of recent years' data as support for the Fixed-Base Percentage computation; actual base-year records must be analyzed. In support of this substantiation standard, ATG Chapter 6 (Footnote 14) cites Research, Inc. v. United States, 95-1 USTC ¶ 50,407 (D. Minn. 1995) (also reported at 1995 WL 560140). Although decided under the pre-1990 "rolling base period" rules—and, as tax legal commentary notes, representing a federal district court holding rather than an automatic invalidation rule for immaterial record gaps—Research, Inc. directly illustrates the evidentiary consequences of failing to substantiate a consistent baseline. There, the taxpayer included expenses for "special system projects" in its credit-year QREs and admitted incurring the same type of project expenses during the base period, but had destroyed the relevant base-period documentation and therefore could not quantify its base-period QREs; the District of Minnesota disallowed the credit because the relative increase in QREs could not be measured without accounting for base-period expenses on the same class of projects. Recent Tax Court jurisprudence continues to reinforce strict base-period substantiation; as Grant Thornton reported in February 2026 regarding George v. Commissioner, when a taxpayer failed to substantiate base-period QREs under the ASC, the Tax Court declined to apply the Cohan rule to estimate base-period QREs and instead restricted the taxpayer to the 6% statutory fallback rate.

Under I.R.C. § 6001, 26 CFR § 1.6001-1, and ATG Chapter 7 (Substantiation and Recordkeeping, updated July 2, 2026), taxpayers bear the affirmative burden of retaining records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate every component of the FBP and Base Amount. At the opening audit meeting, ATG Chapter 7 directs examiners to issue "bite-sized" Information Document Requests (IDRs) with enforced turnaround times specifically requesting the taxpayer's base amount and fixed-base percentage calculations, general information including the chart of accounts and organization charts, and complete records of corporate acquisitions and dispositions from 1984 through the tax year under audit, supplemented where appropriate by annual reports, internal audit submissions, board minutes, project authorizations, and outside consultant studies. Courts permit estimation methods only where contemporaneous records do not exist, and then only if (1) the taxpayer first establishes that it engaged in qualified research activities as defined in IRC § 41(d), (2) the failure to maintain a proper system to capture relevant information is not an "inexactitude of their own making," (3) the sole issue is the exact dollar amount paid or incurred in the qualified research activity, and (4) the taxpayer provides factual support for every assumption underlying its estimates. Where recordkeeping remains deficient, ATG Chapter 7 advises examiners to consider issuing a formal Notice of Inadequate Records under 26 CFR § 1.6001-1(d).
Policy and Compliance Analysis: Recommendations

items: Legislative Reform to Modernize the 1984–1988 Base Period: From a tax administration standpoint, eliminating the requirement to preserve and audit forty-year-old ledgers from 1984–1988 would reduce substantiation disputes under I.R.C. § 6001 while aligning the RRC benchmark with contemporary corporate operations.

Internal Mandate for a Perpetual FBP Historical Compliance File and Utilization of IRS RCRAs: Complementing this internal governance protocol, Large Business and International (formerly Large and Mid-Size Business, LMSB) taxpayers should consider executing a formal Research Credit Recordkeeping Agreement (RCRA) with the IRS pursuant to Notice 2004-11 (published February 9, 2004), which—as highlighted in Chapter 7 of the IRS Audit Techniques Guide—enables the taxpayer and the IRS to agree upfront upon completion of an examination cycle on the exact prospective records required to substantiate future research credit claims.
